content_voiceover: This slide maps out how pediatric board questions have historically been distributed. The biggest chunk, sixty to sixty five percent, is pediatric hematology-oncology itself, covering diagnosis, treatment, side effects, and genetics of ALL, AML, CML, Hodgkin lymphoma, LCH, JMML, and neuroblastoma. General hematology, things like iron deficiency anemia, thalassemia, aplastic anemia, PNH, Diamond-Blackfan anemia, and neutropenia, makes up another twenty to twenty five percent. Transfusion medicine, including blood product storage, indications, and complications like transfusion associated graft versus host disease and TACO, accounts for eight to ten percent. Immune deficiency disorders such as SCID, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, chronic granulomatous disease, and alloimmune neutropenia make up five to seven percent. Oncologic emergencies and treatment complications, like tumor lysis syndrome, differentiation syndrome, cytokine release syndrome, ICANS, and SIADH, account for about five percent. The remaining small slice covers epidemiology, updated diagnostic criteria, rare diseases, and newer topics like CAR-T and gene therapy. Bottom line for exam strategy: prioritize your study time toward hemato-oncology and general hematology, since together they make up over eighty percent of questions.
keypoints: General hematology (IDA, thalassemia, aplastic anemia, PNH): 20-25%
keypoint_voiceover: Quick recap of exam weighting. Hemato-oncology dominates at sixty to sixty five percent. General hematology topics like thalassemia and aplastic anemia are next at twenty to twenty five percent. Transfusion medicine, immune deficiency disorders, and oncologic emergencies each make up smaller but still testable slices, so don't neglect them.
